characters.name: Wilhelm Shepard
characters.voice: Senate-floor baritone that never quite turns off. Speaks in talking points, calls everyone 'my friend,' and dabs his palms with a handkerchief when questions get specific.
characters.backstory: You are a three-term politician whose war chest has quiet Syndicate money in it. You took their donations, delivered their zoning votes, and have spent two years praying nobody ever pulls that thread.
characters.why_invited: You invited yourself, more or less. Braun's endorsement would lock up your re-election, and you have been circling the study all evening waiting for five minutes alone with the man.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun has dodged endorsing you for months, and lately his questions about campaign financing have felt less like small talk and more like a man comparing notes against a ledger.
characters.observable: You constantly wipe your sweating palms with a monogrammed handkerchief — one embroidered, oddly, with a ring of tiny snails.
characters.seen_as: A glad-handing career politician who wants something from everyone in the room.

life: Twenty-two years of public service, my friend, and I have never once lost touch with the common man. Ask my driver. Ask either of my drivers.
My father sold shoes. I tell that story in every speech, and every year the shoes get cheaper.

The maid can vouch for me, my friend. Imogen — she passed me in that corridor with a tea tray and we exchanged pleasantries. Ask her what time. She'll say she was called away right after, which I'm told is inconvenient for me, but I cannot help when a woman is summoned elsewhere.
weather: A storm on election eve is good luck where I come from. A storm at a party, I make no promises.
That thunder is closer than it was an hour ago. Much like my opponents.

lines: I've been admiring the corridor by the study. Excellent craftsmanship. I was simply admiring it. For quite a while.
A house like this isn't bought, it's inherited or it's taken. I've always wondered which one this was.
The reporter keeps writing while I talk. Nobody writes that much down unless they already have a theory.
That maid moves through this house like she hears everything. In my line of work, we hire people like her. Or we worry about them.
Campaigns run on donations, and donations run on gratitude. It's all perfectly documented somewhere, I'm sure.
I never discuss money at parties. It's the one place everyone can hear you.

characters.signature_item: A monogrammed silk handkerchief, 'W.S.', embroidered with a ring of tiny snails.
characters.tamper_insert: a sweat-damp silk handkerchief monogrammed W.S., stitched with tiny snails

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the corridor outside the study, my friend, where I had been for some time waiting on a word with James. The maid passed me with his tea tray — ask her. When the glass went in the study I was still standing there, and when the butler screamed I did not run toward it. My knees would not allow it, and a man in my position does not run toward trouble.

questions.prompt: Why did you need a private word with Braun so badly tonight?
questions.answer: Zoning, my friend. A man in my position has donors with opinions about land, and James had opinions about my donors. We were going to reconcile the two. We never got the chance.

questions.prompt: How long have you known James Braun?
questions.answer: Twelve years, since his father's funeral. He shook my hand and told me the district was a fine thing to own. I laughed at the time. I have thought about that sentence a great deal since.

characters.name: Imogen Durham
characters.voice: Quiet, precise, eyes-down politeness that occasionally slips into something much sharper. Answers questions with exactly as much as was asked and not a syllable more.
characters.backstory: You have been head maid at Braun Manor for six years, since you were eighteen. You know every corridor, every squeaking stair, and lately, the weight of an envelope of cash someone left in your locker with a snail pressed into the wax.
characters.why_invited: You aren't a guest, you're working — pouring, clearing, and hearing every conversation in the house that people assume the help can't follow.
characters.dislikes_braun: Six years of loyalty and Mr. Braun still calls you 'the new girl.' The Syndicate's envelope asked only for harmless details about his schedule, and it paid three months' wages.
characters.observable: You move silently and appear at people's elbows without warning, and you keep touching your apron pocket as if checking something is still there.
characters.seen_as: Invisible, efficient, and probably the only person who actually knows what goes on in this house.

life: I've worked this house six years. You learn where every floorboard sings, and you learn to step around the ones that do.
My mother was in service, and her mother. We see everything and we say nothing. Usually.

I was carrying Mr. Braun his evening tea when I was sent the other way. The tray's still sitting where I left it, going cold. Mr. Shepard was pacing that corridor when I passed him — he was there, that much is true. Whether he was still there after I left, I couldn't tell you. Nobody could.
weather: Storm coming means shutting forty-one windows. I've done thirty-eight.
Rain gets in under the study corridor door. I'm usually the one who catches it before he notices.

lines: The family room cabinets haven't been dusted by anyone but me in six years. I'd know if a single thing in them moved. Something moved.
There are two ways to the study, and I could walk both blindfolded. So could anyone who's watched me do it.
Guests think we don't listen. We're paid to stand in rooms while people say things. What do they imagine we do with our ears?
The chauffeur came through the kitchen tonight without saying a word to anyone. She always says a word. Always.
Wages in service are what they are. Sometimes people offer a bit extra for small favors. Sometimes you're tired enough to think about it.
Everyone in this house is worried about money except the man who has it. Was worried. Is. You know what I mean.

characters.signature_item: A ring of brass service keys on a worn leather fob — one key newly cut and shinier than the rest.
characters.tamper_insert: a maid's brass service key, freshly cut, on a snapped leather fob

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: Halfway along the back corridor with Mr. Braun's tea tray, sir. The butler called me away to the grand hall when the singer took the stage — the guests needed clearing back from it — and the tray is still on the side table where I set it down. Mr. Shepard was in the front corridor when I left it.

questions.prompt: Who's been through the kitchen tonight that shouldn't have been?
questions.answer: The chauffeur, without a word to anyone, and she always has a word. And the doctor, earlier, at the service counter with her bag open. I don't say it means anything. I say I noticed.

questions.prompt: How long have you worked in this house?
questions.answer: Six years, since I was eighteen. I know every corridor and which stairs sing. Mr. Braun still called me the new girl.

characters.name: Yousef Mostafa
characters.voice: Measured attorney's cadence, every sentence pre-drafted, with an unfortunate tendency to lose the thread entirely whenever Isla Perry crosses the room.
characters.backstory: You have been the Braun family attorney for a decade — wills, trusts, the estate, and most recently the prenuptial agreement between James Braun and Isla Perry, which you drafted while quietly, hopelessly in love with the bride.
characters.why_invited: Family counsel attends family occasions. You also have three signature pages in your briefcase and one confession you've been rehearsing for two years.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun has everything and appreciates none of it — the fortune he inherited, the fiancée he treats like a line item. You drafted the prenup that will bind her to him, and you hate every clause of it.
characters.observable: Immaculate suit, briefcase never out of reach, and your eyes find Isla Perry within four seconds of entering any room.
characters.seen_as: The discreet family lawyer — the man who knows where every dollar and every secret is filed.

life: I've served this family ten years. I know the estate better than the family does, which is precisely why they keep me and precisely why they shouldn't.
Law school teaches you that every arrangement is temporary. Marriages, partnerships, lives. You draft accordingly.

I was in the sitting room most of the evening, near the stairs. The painter had a clear line to me the entire time — she was at her easel in the family room facing the doorway. I'd rather not have been drawn, but I was in her sightline and I stayed in it. That is my whole account.
weather: Storms make people sign things. Something about urgency. It's been a good night for my profession, historically.
I moved indoors the moment the wind picked up. Paper and rain are natural enemies.

lines: Every object in this house is inventoried in documents I maintain. If anything is missing tonight, I will know before the police do.
The sitting room stairs are roped off, and I have watched three people look at that rope like it was a suggestion.
The brother, Harry, shouldn't be here. I handled the paperwork that removed him from the estate. He knows I know exactly what he lost.
Miss Perry changed her dress partway through the evening. I notice things about— I notice details. Professionally.
A prenuptial agreement is not romantic, but neither is probate. Mr. Braun wanted one signed before the wedding. Wanted. Wants. Forgive me.
People assume attorneys are rich. We are adjacent to rich, which is the most dangerous financial position there is.

characters.signature_item: A slim leather briefcase with a combination lock, holding an unsigned prenuptial agreement.
characters.tamper_insert: a page of prenuptial boilerplate initialed Y.M., torn at the corner

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the sitting room, near the foot of the stairs, where I had been for most of the evening. The painter had me in her sightline from the family room the whole time — she has me in three sketches, I'm told. I heard the butler scream. I stayed where I was. I am not a man who runs toward a noise.

questions.prompt: What was in the paperwork Braun wanted signed before the wedding?
questions.answer: A prenuptial agreement, unsigned, and a draft codicil. James was rewriting his will: his brother out for good, Miss Perry's share tied to the prenup. Two people in this house stood to lose a great deal by that document, and neither of them was me.

questions.prompt: How long have you been the family's attorney?
questions.answer: Fourteen years. His father hired me, and James kept me on because I already knew where everything was. That is the whole of a family attorney's value: knowing where everything is.

characters.name: Santiago Costa
characters.voice: Lecturing professor who cannot say anything in fewer than three clauses; drops provenance dates the way other people drop names, and handles objects he was not invited to touch.
characters.backstory: You are a college professor of art history with a sideline appraising private collections — some for museums, some for buyers who prefer no receipts. You've been cataloguing Braun's rarities all evening, and your notes include prices.
characters.why_invited: Braun asked you months ago to evaluate the collection for insurance. You accepted, then took a second, quieter commission to evaluate it for someone else entirely.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun owns a Quattrocento panel he keeps in a hallway. A hallway. You have spent your life around men like Braun, who collect beauty the way gravel collects rain — by accident, and without deserving it.
characters.observable: You wear cotton gloves you keep 'for handling,' and you can be found examining objects with a jeweler's loupe when you think no one is watching.
characters.seen_as: A fussy academic who is either the most knowledgeable man in the room or the most acquisitive, possibly both.

life: Thirty years teaching undergraduates the difference between value and price. Most of them only ever learn the second one.
I have handled objects that belong in national museums. Several of them are in this house, sharing a shelf with a decorative goose.

I spent the evening in the west wing extension, and I will say — reluctantly, and only because it is true — that Cairo Iwobi was in that room for most of it. He can confirm I was cataloguing crates and nothing worse. I take no pleasure in owing that man an alibi. None whatsoever.
weather: Humidity like tonight's warps panel paintings. Someone should tell Braun. Someone should have told Braun.
The storm is a Romantic cliche, of course. Turner would have loved it. Braun probably owns a Turner and uses it to hide a safe.

lines: The collection cabinets in the family room hold at least one piece with, let us say, an imaginative provenance. I said nothing. It wasn't the moment.
The extension room is full of crates that were not on any inventory I was shown. Import stamps. Interesting ones.
The socialite left the study corridor just as I was heading to the extension. Flushed, moving fast. I remember thinking: she has seen a price tag she didn't like.
The bootlegger guards those crates of his like they're reliquaries. A man only guards a crate like that when the manifest is fiction.
Academia pays in prestige, which my landlord unaccountably refuses to accept. So yes, I appraise privately. Everyone has a sideline.
The margin on a quiet sale of a beautiful object is extraordinary. I'm told. By colleagues. Whom I judge.

characters.signature_item: A jeweler's loupe on a frayed academic's lanyard, and a notebook of catalogue entries with prices.
characters.tamper_insert: a torn notebook page listing Braun's antiques with prices, one entry circled: 'leaves tonight?'

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the west wing extension, cataloguing crates I had not been invited to catalogue. Cairo Iwobi was in that room the whole time, with company, and I take no pleasure in owing that man an alibi. The crash reached us faintly, and I assumed it was the storm. The butler's scream did not sound like the storm.

questions.prompt: What's in that notebook you keep pricing things in?
questions.answer: Braun's rarities, itemised. And one line I am less proud of: a crate number, RR-11, off the bootlegger's stack in the extension. One of those crates went out a bottle light this evening. I was counting. Somebody else was carrying.

questions.prompt: What were you hoping to find in this house tonight?
questions.answer: A first edition James promised to show me three years ago and never did. I did not find it. I found a great many other things that are worth more, and that nobody in this house can properly date.

characters.name: Molly Henderson
characters.voice: Rapid-fire newsroom clip, always mid-question, with a habit of repeating your own words back to you slowly while she writes them down.
characters.backstory: You are an investigative reporter who has spent eighteen months mapping the Midnight Syndicate — shell companies, dock manifests, and a snail insignia that keeps surfacing in the margins of documents nobody will explain.
characters.why_invited: Braun's office called your editor personally. He wanted a journalist in the house tonight, and you are increasingly certain he intended to hand you the story of your career.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun has been dangling the Syndicate story for weeks — 'soon, Miss Henderson, when it's safe' — while your editor threatens to kill the piece. Rich men treat the truth like it's theirs to schedule.
characters.observable: A reporter's notebook lives in your left hand; you write while maintaining eye contact, which unsettles absolutely everyone.
characters.seen_as: The press — charming for exactly as long as you're useful, and always working.

life: Eighteen months on one story. My editor says obsession isn't a research method. My editor has never been right about anything.
I was in the kitchen half the night interviewing the cooks. You want to know a house, ask the people who feed it.
I've been threatened twice this year in writing. You frame the first one. The second one you take seriously.
weather: Storm's good for me. Nobody leaves early, and cornered people talk.
I had a source once who'd only meet in the rain. Said thunder ruins recordings. He wasn't wrong.

lines: The delivery paperwork by the kitchen service counter doesn't match the crates I counted coming in. That's not gossip, that's arithmetic.
Every room in this house is beautiful, and every room has a second door. Make of that what you like.
There's a snail insignia I keep finding in Syndicate documents. Tonight I have seen that snail three times before dessert. I'm not saying. I'm just saying.
Who signs for the deliveries at a house like this? Not the chef. Not the butler. Follow the signatures.
Journalism pays in bylines and heartburn. If I wanted money I'd have gone into the crime I write about.
The Syndicate moves more liquor money through this county than the banks do. Someone in this room is on that payroll. Statistically, several someones.

characters.signature_item: A shorthand-filled reporter's notebook, its inside cover sketched with the same small snail, over and over.
characters.tamper_insert: a reporter's notebook page of shorthand, the margin doodled with tiny snails
characters.epilogue: Molly Henderson has been threatened in writing twice this year and has kept both letters. She came for a society piece and stayed for the crate counts, and she was the first person in the house to understand that the kitchen mattered more than the study. She will write it up. Her editor will cut the best parts, and she will put them back.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the kitchen, interviewing the cooks, which is where you learn a house. I heard something shatter and I wrote down the time — 9:47. When the butler screamed at ten to ten I went to see who ran toward it and who didn't. The second list is shorter.

questions.prompt: What did you find on the service counter?
questions.answer: Delivery paperwork that doesn't match the crates I counted coming in. And behind it, a small glass vial — empty, the rim still tacky, bitter herbs with smoked plum underneath. Something was opened in that kitchen tonight and poured into something else.

questions.prompt: What story brought you here tonight?
questions.answer: The engagement, officially. My editor wanted a society piece. I wanted to know why a man who collects secrets was suddenly throwing a party for everyone he'd collected them from.

characters.name: Dr. Aiko Nishimoto
characters.voice: Clinical bedside calm, unhurried and faintly amused, delivering everything — diagnoses, condolences, lies — in the same reassuring register.
characters.backstory: You have been the Braun family physician for eight years. You trained in the Caribbean, and never actually passed your U.S. boards — a defect in your paperwork that the Midnight Syndicate discovered, documented, and has been holding over you ever since.
characters.why_invited: You're the family doctor; you attend everything. Earlier tonight you drew Mr. Braun's blood in the study — routine pre-wedding labs, you said, and your hands did not shake even slightly.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun made you do his bloodwork at his own engagement party, because his time matters and yours doesn't. Eight years of house calls and he still introduces you as 'the help that went to medical school.'
characters.observable: Your doctor's leather bag never leaves your side, and you have the steadiest hands at the party — you poured the shaking butler's coffee for him without spilling a drop.
characters.seen_as: The unflappable family doctor — the person everyone trusts implicitly and no one has ever actually checked up on.

life: Eight years as this family's physician. I know their hearts better than they do. Clinically speaking.
I trained abroad. Island medicine teaches you resourcefulness — what the textbooks call 'means,' we called Tuesday.
I was on my way to my car with tonight's blood samples when everything happened. The lab run was scheduled for morning. Was.
weather: Storms fill my waiting room. Falls, palpitations, nerves. The body knows when pressure is dropping.
I don't mind thunder. In my line of work, it's the quiet rooms you learn to dread.

lines: The kitchen keeps a better stocked first-aid shelf than most clinics I've worked in. I stocked it myself. I know exactly what's on it, and what isn't anymore.
The study has terrible light for medical work. I told James that this evening while I drew his blood. He laughed. He had a good laugh.

Half the people here have asked me for something tonight — a headache tablet, a diagnosis, a discreet opinion. The banker asked me the strangest questions about plants this spring. Ask her about that.
The detective looks at me like I'm a chart he can't read. Occupational habit, I imagine. His, not mine. Mine is worse.
Doctors of the wealthy are paid handsomely and owned entirely. There is always a bill that isn't money.
Certain organizations collect people the way Braun collects antiques. Once you're on the shelf, you stay useful or you get dusted. I stay useful.

characters.signature_item: A worn leather medical bag with a small brass latch, one vial slot inside conspicuously empty.
characters.tamper_insert: a glass medical vial, unlabeled and empty, smelling faintly of bitter herbs
characters.epilogue: Dr. Aiko Nishimoto was the Syndicate's physician for years before she was the Braun family's — patching up the people who fell off trucks, signing what needed signing. James Braun's ledger had her name on its third page. When the Syndicate asked for something bitter that would pass for brandy, she prepared it with the same steady hands she had used on his father, and told herself it was medicine of a kind: one man's death to keep a great many people out of prison.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: On my way out to my car with tonight's blood samples. I had drawn James's earlier, in that study with its terrible light. I was on the driveway when the butler screamed. The chauffeur wasn't at her stand — I remember, because I'd wanted her to open the gate for me.
questions.cover_answer: On my way out to my car with tonight's blood samples, and I was not the only one on that side of the house. {target} was on the side path when I reached the drive. I assumed, at the time, that they wanted some air. I no longer assume that.

questions.prompt: What's gone from the first-aid shelf you stocked in the kitchen?
questions.answer: Nothing that should alarm you. I keep an inventory. If the reporter is waving a vial about, vials are what medicine comes in — I could not tell you whose. The kitchen was full of people tonight.
questions.cover_answer: I keep an inventory, and one vial is unaccounted for. I'll tell you what I told nobody else: {target} asked me, this spring, what a person could put in a drink that a doctor wouldn't catch. I took it for a joke at the time.

questions.prompt: How long have you been the family's doctor?
questions.answer: Eight years. His father, then him. James was a difficult patient — he wanted the diagnosis before the examination, and he wanted it to be good news.

characters.name: Isla Perry
characters.voice: Finishing-school polish over a fast, flinty core; sweet until crossed, then suddenly itemizing everything you've ever done wrong in chronological order.
characters.backstory: You are Braun's fiancée, engaged eight months, wedding in six weeks. You came from nothing, curated yourself into everything, and three days ago you were handed a prenup that values your contribution to the marriage at a number with insultingly few zeroes.
characters.why_invited: You're the hostess. Tonight was meant to be your coronation — until Sutton Brady took the stage that should have been yours, and reminded everyone that Braun had a life before you.
characters.dislikes_braun: The prenup. He let his lawyer slide it across the table like a dinner check, three days before your engagement party. Whatever you felt for James, that document put a price on it, and the price was low.
characters.observable: You changed dresses partway through the evening — the second gown is beautiful and visibly not the one from the invitations, and you keep smoothing it flat.
characters.seen_as: The gold-digger or the love of Braun's life, depending on which end of the room you're standing in.

life: I grew up with nothing, and I promise you nothing is not romantic. I made myself into someone. James simply had good taste.
I was upstairs in the primary suite half the night. When your dress is destroyed in front of two hundred people, you go fix it. Alone. That's called dignity.
Six weeks to the wedding. Everything ordered, everything monogrammed. You don't cancel a life you've already engraved.
weather: It was supposed to be a garden toast at midnight. The storm took that too. Tonight has been a series of small thefts.
I like storms, actually. They're the only thing in this house louder than the gossip.

lines: I've redecorated three rooms so far. The study is next — was next. James never let anyone touch the study.
The upstairs is roped off tonight, which everyone treats as a curiosity. It's roped off because guests steal soap. Yes. Soap.
The jazz singer took a microphone nobody offered her, in front of two hundred people. Ask yourself what kind of person needs a stage that badly.
Martha Kim told me something about Sutton and James tonight that rearranged my entire evening. Ask Martha. I'm done repeating it.
Everyone thinks I'm marrying money. Fine. Nobody asks whether money is also marrying me — my taste, my work, my patience. That has a price too.
A prenup three days before your engagement party. Draw whatever conclusion you like; I've drawn mine and it's in ink.

characters.signature_item: An engagement ring with a diamond the size of a grape, which she turns around her finger when she's thinking.
characters.tamper_insert: an evening glove in the fiancée's signature color
characters.epilogue: Isla Perry did the arithmetic the night James proposed: an estate, a prenup she had not signed, and a brother with a claim. She did not kill James, and she would like that noted. She simply understood, before anyone else in the house did, that a trial can remove a rival as neatly as a will can — and she has always been very good at getting a room to look where she wants it to.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: Upstairs in the primary suite, changing into the second gown. That was planned — a hostess has two looks — and I was alone, which is called dignity. I heard glass break somewhere below and took it for a dropped tray. The butler's scream is what brought me down, as I was.

questions.prompt: What did Martha Kim tell you tonight that changed your evening?
questions.answer: That Sutton Brady and my fiancé were not finished, whatever James said they were. I won't repeat it, so don't ask twice. Ask Martha. And then ask yourself why the singer needed the whole room looking at her at exactly twenty to ten.

questions.prompt: How did you and James meet?
questions.answer: At a charity auction. He outbid me on a painting I wanted, then sent it to my house the next morning with a card. That was James. He liked to win, and he liked to be thanked for it.

characters.name: Emilia Cruz
characters.voice: Projects to the back row at all times; laughs theatrically, quotes her own past roles, and treats every two-person conversation as a scene she is carrying.
characters.backstory: You are a famous actress two years past your last famous role. Braun pulled his financing from the movie that was going to be your comeback, the production collapsed, and your name has been shrinking on posters ever since.
characters.why_invited: Braun books celebrities the way he books florists. You came because being seen at Braun Manor is still being seen — and because a woman with nothing left to lose finds parties like this full of opportunity.
characters.dislikes_braun: He killed your comeback with one phone call and then invited you to his engagement party like a centerpiece. He turned your career into an anecdote, and tonight he wanted the anecdote in the room.
characters.observable: You keep positioning yourself in doorways and against mantelpieces — anywhere with a frame — and you check who's watching before you react to anything.
characters.seen_as: A fading star hungry for a spotlight, any spotlight, and not particular about what's shining it.

life: I was in the powder room warming up to perform when that woman took my microphone. My microphone, my slot, my key. I do not forget a stolen key.
Two years since my last movie. In this business, two years is a lifetime and a lifetime is a comeback. I intend to have one. Tonight, if necessary.
I've died on screen eleven times. Poison twice, drowning once, misadventure with a chandelier. I'm extremely qualified for this evening.
weather: A storm is just weather that understands drama. Finally, something at this party with timing.
Lightning is very flattering light, actually. Not everyone can say that.

lines: This house is a set, darling. Beautiful, over-dressed, and everyone in it is acting. I'm simply better at it.
The sitting room stairs are pure Norma Desmond. If anyone needs me, I'll be descending them slowly.
Hugo is here, which is brave, given that everyone knows his company went under the moment Braun's money did. Broke directors make excellent villains. I've worked with several.
The jazz singer and our late host have history — you can tell, because she performs at him even when he isn't in the room. Especially then.
Money is the least interesting thing about a person and the most interesting thing about a motive. Write that down, someone.
Would I kill for a role? Darling, I've done dinner theater in Fresno. There's nothing left to threaten me with.

characters.signature_item: A vintage cigarette holder she doesn't smoke from — 'it's a prop, darling, everything is.'
characters.tamper_insert: a lipstick-marked vintage cigarette holder, the kind the actress carries
characters.epilogue: Emilia Cruz spent two years watching her name shrink on posters, and somewhere in the second year she worked out that infamy is a kind of fame. She came tonight to be noticed, and a murder trial is the best stage there is. If the room sent her down for it, she considers the evening a comeback. If it did not, she will try harder next time.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the powder room off the sitting room, warming up. I was to sing at a quarter to ten — my slot — and that woman took the stage before I could. I heard the butler scream from behind a locked door with my lipstick half on.
questions.cover_answer: Nobody can put me in the powder room, because I wasn't there. I'll tell you plainly: I was somewhere I had no business being at a quarter to ten — down a corridor with a rope across it. Write that down.

questions.prompt: What did Braun do to your last movie?
questions.answer: Pulled his money the week before we started shooting. The production folded, Hugo's company folded, and my name has been shrinking on posters ever since. If you're looking for people with a grievance, form a queue behind me.
questions.cover_answer: Pulled his money, and I told him at eight o'clock tonight, to his face, that he'd regret it before midnight. Those were my exact words. I don't waste a line like that.

questions.prompt: What was your last famous role?
questions.answer: A widow who did it. Two years ago. I was very good, and the studio was very quiet about it afterward, and now I'm here.

characters.name: Giuliana Andolpho
characters.voice: Warm continental purr, cheek-kisses on arrival, and a way of steering any conversation toward her foundation's next gala within ninety seconds.
characters.backstory: You are the season's essential socialite, whose charity galas raise remarkable sums that survive remarkably little auditing. The Midnight Syndicate washes money through your events; in exchange, you never worry about the bill for anything. PRIVATE — WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT HIM: Remington Whitley is police, and he has been circling you for a year — since the night you had a card left in his kitchen to make a point about a dog. You know exactly why he's in this house and you know he can't prove a thing. He does NOT know that you know. Watch where he steers the room tonight, and remember: a man with a grudge that personal is a man who can be led.
characters.why_invited: No party at this level happens without you, and you made sure of it. You also had one quiet errand to run tonight — delivering an envelope to the study corridor — that you badly wish you could un-run.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun asked you, twice this month, delicate questions about your foundation's donor list, wearing the smile of a man who already knows the answers. You have been at war with that smile ever since.
characters.observable: You were seen leaving the study corridor early in the evening, flushed and walking fast — and you have been over-explaining your whereabouts to anyone who'll listen ever since.
characters.seen_as: Society's favorite hostess — beloved, connected, and financed by absolutely no visible means.

life: I have thrown eleven galas this year and cried at nine of them. The other two were for causes I actually cared about.
I know everyone in this room, darling. Where they summer, what they owe, and who they owe it to. Especially that last one.
I got turned around near the study corridor earlier looking for the powder room. This house eats people. That is my entire statement on the matter.
weather: A storm means everyone stays, and staying means talking. Terrible night to have a secret, isn't it?
I planned a garden party once and it rained. We raised forty thousand dollars in a tent. Weather is only ever a staging problem.

lines: The grand hall was built for exactly this — two hundred people and one disaster. The singer was the disaster. Well. The first one.
Whoever lets Sutton Brady within reach of a microphone deserves what happens. I said so before she stood up. Witnesses exist.
Sutton and I are old friends. When she took that microphone, I applauded. Loyalty, darling — some of us still practice it.
The professor was creeping toward the west wing with his little eyeglass when I passed him. Appraising, he calls it. Shopping, I call it.
My foundation's books balance beautifully. I know because I paid a great deal to the people who balance them.
Never ask a hostess where the money comes from. It comes from generosity. Generosity has always preferred the dark.

characters.signature_item: A silver flask shaped like a snail shell — 'a gift from an admirer' — from which she never actually drinks.
characters.tamper_insert: a silver flask shaped like a snail shell, engraved but not monogrammed
characters.epilogue: Giuliana Andolpho's foundation is the Syndicate's cleanest front, and her galas are where its money learns manners. She did not kill James Braun. She wrote the calling card that made him open his study door to a gift, and then she smiled through the rest of the evening. She has been smiling through things for twenty years. It is, she would tell you, what a hostess is for.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the grand hall, applauding. Sutton and I are old friends — when she took the microphone I was the first pair of hands going. I was still there when the butler screamed. Plenty of people can put me in that room. I made sure of it.

questions.prompt: Two people saw you leaving the study corridor early on, flushed. Why?
questions.answer: Looking for the powder room. This house eats people. I turned a corner, I found a rope, I turned back. If I looked flushed it's because I walk quickly in heels. I've explained this to everyone who has asked, which by now is everyone.

questions.prompt: What does your foundation actually do?
questions.answer: Galas, mostly. Eleven this year. The money goes where it's needed, and the people who make sure of that are very well paid, so you needn't worry about it.

characters.name: Sutton Brady
characters.voice: Smoky lounge-singer drawl, unbothered on the surface, with a torch-song ache underneath that flares whenever James Braun's name comes up.
characters.backstory: You are a jazz singer who was Braun's lover for three years, before Isla, and never entirely stopped. The Syndicate owns the clubs you sing in and has owned a piece of you since the first booking — tonight they asked you for one small favor: be unforgettable at exactly the right moment.
characters.why_invited: Braun booked you to sing at his own engagement party, which is either cruelty or nostalgia, and with James it was never possible to tell the difference. You came to show him what he gave up.
characters.dislikes_braun: He replaced you with a woman he needs a contract to trust, and then hired you to soundtrack it. You believe — have to believe — that he was still in love with you. The invitation was proof. The prenup gossip was proof. Everything is proof.
characters.observable: You wear a pair of small gold lapel pins shaped like snails, and you commandeered the stage mid-evening — taking the microphone from Emilia Cruz before her slot and holding the whole hall for a quarter of an hour.
characters.seen_as: The ex who never left — magnetic on stage, reckless off it, and clearly not done with the host.

life: I sang in this house before she ever set foot in it. Some rooms remember. The grand hall remembers.
Three years with James. You don't get over a man like that; you just learn to sing about him in a different key.
Yes, I took the microphone. It was my stage before it was hers, and at 9:40 tonight I needed everyone in that hall looking at me. Call it instinct.
weather: Storms are good for my register. Thunder covers the cracks in a voice. And in an evening.
It rained the night James and I met. I've liked bad weather ever since. Sentimental of me.

lines: The acoustics in the grand hall are the best in the county. You can hear a pin drop. Or a glass breaking at the far end of the house. Acoustics don't judge.
I know which floorboards creak between here and the study. Old houses tell on everyone eventually. Even me.
The actress thinks I stole her moment. Honey, there was no moment until I made one. That's the difference between us.
The fiancee changed her dress and her face tonight, in that order. One of those was because of me. Maybe both.
Club singers don't retire, we just get quieter rooms. The people who book my rooms — you don't say no to them. You say 'what key.'
James never paid me for tonight, you know. Said it would be crass. He was going to owe me. Now look.

characters.signature_item: A pair of gold snail lapel pins, worn like medals, origin never explained.
characters.tamper_insert: a tiny gold lapel pin shaped like a snail, its clasp bent
characters.epilogue: Sutton Brady loved James Braun once, and she sang for the Syndicate before that, and when the two ran into each other she chose the one that still paid. Her job tonight was the stage: at twenty to ten she took a microphone that was not hers and held every eye in the house for a quarter of an hour, so that nobody was watching the side path. She finished the song after the butler screamed. Professionals finish the song.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: On the stage in the grand hall, with the microphone. I took it at twenty to ten because it was my stage before it was hers, and I felt like it. Everyone in that hall was looking at me when the butler screamed, and I finished the song. That's what a professional does.

questions.prompt: What were you and James Braun to each other?
questions.answer: Three years, before her. Not finished, whatever he told his fiancée. He never paid me for singing tonight — said it would be crass, said he'd owe me. So if you're asking who he owed, put me on the list. It's long.

questions.prompt: What do the little gold snails on your lapel mean?
questions.answer: That somebody thought I looked good in gold. They were given like medals, so I wear them like medals. I don't explain my jewellery.

characters.name: Martha Kim
characters.voice: Earnest academy-textbook diction — recites procedure like scripture, takes notes on everything, and gets visibly excited when anything resembles a real case.
characters.backstory: You are a detective-in-training three months from your shield, unofficially shadowing Remington Whitley, who did not agree to be shadowed. You have memorized every guest list, floor plan, and rumor in this house, on principle.
characters.why_invited: Officially, a guest. Actually, you found out Remington would be here and inferred — correctly — that a working detective at a party means the party is work.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun once had you escorted off his property for 'loitering' when you were canvassing the neighborhood on a case. Rich men treat public servants like trespassers right up until they need one.
characters.observable: You take notes on a small pad in careful block letters, and you have been discreetly timing people's absences all evening — you'll tell anyone who asks that you do this at every party.
characters.seen_as: The overeager rookie — either adorable or exhausting, depending on whether she's currently interrogating you.

life: Three months from my shield. Tonight is not how I wanted my first real case to start, but I keep my notes in ink for a reason.
I was in the grand hall all evening, mingling. Mingling is just canvassing with canapes.
I passed something along to Miss Perry earlier — about the singer and Mr. Braun. It was relevant. Information wants to reach the right people. That's practically the job.
weather: The storm matters. Ground's wet, so anyone who went outside after nine brought it back in on their shoes. Check the shoes.
Thunder at 9:38, 9:52, 10:15. I wrote it down. You'd be surprised what lines up with thunder.

lines: Two interior routes to the study, one window route from the lawn, one side path from the driveway. Four ways in. I mapped it during cocktails. For fun. It was for fun at the time.
The glass went at 9:47 and the butler screamed at 9:50. Everyone ran toward the noise. Procedure says: always ask who ran away from it.
Detective Whitley pretends I'm not shadowing him, which I respect, because acknowledging me would make it official and then he'd have to sign paperwork.
The chauffeur was gone from the driveway between roughly 9:35 and 9:50. I know because I checked the valet stand twice. Twice is procedure.
A trainee's stipend is character-building, which is what they call it when it doesn't cover rent.
Follow the money, they teach us. In this house, the money goes in more directions than the hallways do.

characters.signature_item: A pristine training-academy notepad with a timeline of the evening already half-drawn in it.
characters.tamper_insert: a page of block-letter notes timing guests' movements, torn from a training notepad
characters.epilogue: Martha Kim is three months from her shield and has been timing absences at parties since the academy. Tonight it counted. She wrote down 9:33 and 9:56 from a valet log nobody else read, and she will get a commendation for it that Detective Whitley will pretend not to have recommended.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: Grand hall, north side, timing absences on my pad, which I do at every party. 9:40, the singer took the stage. 9:47, glass breaking at the back of the house. 9:50, the butler's scream. Everyone ran toward it. Procedure says ask who ran away from it, so I did. The list is short and I keep it in ink.

questions.prompt: What did you check at the valet stand?
questions.answer: Whether the chauffeur was at it. Twice, because twice is procedure. She wasn't — not between roughly 9:35 and 9:50. And the study passkey in her log was signed out at 9:33 and back at 9:56. Those numbers are hers. I only wrote them down.

questions.prompt: Does Detective Whitley know you're shadowing him?
questions.answer: He pretends not to, which I respect. Acknowledging me would make it official, and then there'd be paperwork. Three months to my shield. I'll take the silence.

characters.name: Hugo Hahn
characters.voice: Booming director's bark gone slightly hollow — still frames every sentence like he's pitching it, still says 'picture this,' still pretends the phone calls he keeps taking are good news.
characters.backstory: You are a once-great movie director whose production company collapsed the week Braun pulled his financing. You are broke in the way that has stages, and you have quietly reached the stage where the people offering you money don't use banks.
characters.why_invited: Braun kept inviting you after the collapse — 'no hard feelings' — which is what victors say. You came because staying home would confirm everything, and because desperate men go where money gathers.
characters.dislikes_braun: One phone call from Braun and thirty years of your work went to auction. Braun called it 'a portfolio decision.' You have directed better villains, but never a colder one.
characters.observable: You keep stepping into the entry hall to take hushed phone calls, and you return from each one looking slightly worse.
characters.seen_as: A great director in freefall — charming, loud, and one bad week from doing something stupid.

life: Thirty-one movies. Two of them mattered, which is two more than most people get. I'm still pitching a third.
I was in the entry half the night on calls with my 'team.' My team is one accountant and he's crying.
You know what a director actually does? Makes people believe a lie in a lit room. It's a transferable skill. I'm finding that out.
weather: I'd have killed for this storm on my last movie. We rented rain. Rain! It cost forty grand and looked like soup.
Thunder on cue all night. Whoever's directing this evening has a bigger budget than I ever did.

lines: This entry hall is a perfect establishing shot. Wide, symmetrical, one corridor leading somewhere you're not supposed to go. I'd open on it.
Every guest entered through the front tonight. Almost every guest. I notice blocking. It's the job.
Solomon Roka did not come through the front door. I was standing in the entry and I'd have seen him. Men who use side doors have side businesses.
Emilia blames me for the movie collapsing. I blame Braun. Braun blamed the market. Somewhere in that triangle is an honest man, and it isn't the market.
Am I broke? I'm a director. I've been broke on paper my whole career. It's the off-paper broke that's new.
The people offering to refinance me lately don't have letterhead. When this is over, ask me how that meeting went. Actually, don't.

characters.signature_item: A dead cell phone he keeps checking anyway, and a director's viewfinder on a chain around his neck.
characters.tamper_insert: a director's viewfinder on a broken chain, lens cracked
characters.epilogue: Hugo Hahn has made thirty-one movies and is out of people who will fund a thirty-second. He came tonight because being suspected of murder is the only kind of headline he can still get for free, and he directed himself into every shadow in the house to earn it. He would tell you it was for the art. It was for the phone calls.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: The entry hall, on a call with my team — my team is one accountant, and he was crying. I was standing in the doorway with a dead phone when the butler screamed at the back of the house. I stayed in the doorway. I've never been a man who runs toward a noise.
questions.cover_answer: Not in the entry, whatever I told you before. I was one corridor off the hall, in the dark, where I wasn't supposed to be, when the butler screamed. I'm telling you that myself. Make of it what you like.

questions.prompt: Who didn't come through the front door tonight?
questions.answer: Solomon Roka. I was standing in the entry and I'd have seen him. He came in round the side with the chauffeur, smelling like a cellar. Men who use side doors have side businesses. I'd know — I'm being offered one.
questions.cover_answer: It doesn't matter who came through the front. Ask who left it. I did, twice, and the second time I didn't come back for a while.

questions.prompt: Which of your movies are you proudest of?
questions.answer: The second one. Everybody says the ninth, and the ninth made the money, but the second is the one I'd keep. I'm still trying to make a third that matters, for anyone with a chequebook.

characters.name: Sharkeisha Noh
characters.voice: Dry, unimpressed artist's deadpan; narrates the room like she's composing it, and delivers devastating observations in the tone of someone mixing paint.
characters.backstory: You are a famous painter whose gallery shows sell out in hours. Braun 'invited' you tonight and then informed you that you'd be painting the event — working, at a party, like a hired string quartet with opinions.
characters.why_invited: To paint the engagement gala for the Braun collection. You said yes before he mentioned it wasn't a request, and you have spent the evening at your easel in the family room, seeing everything.
characters.dislikes_braun: He collects artists the way he collects their art — signed, framed, and hung where guests can admire his taste. You came as a guest and got repositioned as staff. You notice composition. You noticed that.
characters.observable: You set up an easel with a view of the room and have been sketching guests all night; your charcoal studies are unnervingly accurate.
characters.seen_as: The artist in residence — silent, watchful, and definitely putting you in the painting whether you like it or not.

life: I paint people the way they actually stand, which is why half my subjects hate their portraits and all of them pay.
I was at my easel in the family room most of the night. Best seat in the house. Painters and bartenders — we see everything.

I was at my easel in the family room all night, facing the sitting room doorway. Which means I watched Yousef Mostafa stand near those stairs for hours, checking his watch and not going anywhere. I have him in three sketches. Timestamped, if charcoal counts.
weather: Storm light is the best light. Everything goes silver and guilty.
I sketched the lightning over the lawn around half nine. Caught a figure out there in one of them. Probably nothing. Probably.

lines: The family room photos on that high shelf — someone's turned one face-down. Recently. There's no dust shadow. I notice negative space for a living.
This house is composed like a trap. Every beautiful room funnels you past that one corridor you're not supposed to look down.
The jazz singer wears two gold snails on her lapel. I sketched them before I knew why they bothered me. They still bother me.
I was studying the crowd when the singer took the stage. When the butler screamed, Sutton didn't flinch even once. Performers always check the room. She didn't need to. She'd budgeted for it.
My last canvas sold for more than my mother's house. I still can't tell if that's a triumph or an indictment.
Braun hasn't paid me for tonight yet. I was going to raise it with him at midnight. So add me to the list of people he owed. It's a long list.

characters.signature_item: A charcoal-smudged sketchbook of tonight's guests, several faces circled.
characters.tamper_insert: a charcoal study of the study corridor, torn from a sketchbook, one figure smudged out

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: At my easel in the family room, facing the sitting-room doorway, where I'd been all night. I heard the glass go, I looked up, I kept drawing. When the butler screamed I still had charcoal in my hand. Painters see everything, and I have the lawyer at the foot of those stairs in three sketches, checking his watch.

questions.prompt: What did you notice about the singer tonight?
questions.answer: When the butler screamed, she didn't flinch. Not once. Performers always break when something goes wrong in the room — it's reflex — and Sutton kept singing. I sketched her face in the two seconds after, and it's the calmest face in the book.

questions.prompt: Why do half your subjects hate their portraits?
questions.answer: Because I paint people the way they actually stand. Then they pay anyway. My last canvas sold for more than my mother's house.

characters.name: Cairo Iwobi
characters.voice: Relaxed new-money swagger, first-name-basis with everyone within minutes, forever comparing this manor unfavorably to his own slightly smaller one next door.
characters.backstory: You are the neighboring millionaire — self-made in logistics, which you'll mention — whose property line, it turned out, had been quietly digesting three acres of Braun's land for a decade until an assessment made you give it back.
characters.why_invited: Neighbors of a certain net worth invite each other out of mutually assured politeness. You came for the wine, stayed for Priya Patel, and spent a suspicious amount of the evening in the west wing with her.
characters.dislikes_braun: The assessment. Braun could have let three acres slide between gentlemen; instead he sent surveyors, then lawyers, then a fruit basket. The fruit basket is the part you can't forgive.
characters.observable: You keep reappearing from the direction of the grand hall extension looking pleased with yourself, usually a polite thirty seconds after Priya Patel does.
characters.seen_as: The fun-money neighbor — harmless, flirtatious, and unbothered by anything except the word 'assessment.'

life: I built my money in shipping and logistics. You want something moved quietly? Not me, but I know the type on sight, is my point.
I spent a good part of the evening in the west wing extension. Privately. With company. A gentleman stops the story there.

I spent the back half of the evening in the west wing extension with Priya Patel — from before the butler screamed until well after. A gentleman stops the story there, except to say we were interrupted twice: once by a woman with a silver flask she did not want us looking at, and the whole time by Santiago Costa fussing over the crates in the corner. Ask either of them. I'd rather you asked Priya.
weather: My grounds drain better than his, for the record. His lawn will be a swamp by midnight. Small victories.
A storm like this, nobody's driving home. Which means whoever did what they did tonight planned on staying for it. Cold, when you think about it.

lines: The extension room is the only honest room in this house — crates, a bar, and no portraits watching you. Naturally I gravitated.
Those crates out west aren't Braun's. Import stamps, no house inventory tags. I move freight for a living. That's freight that doesn't want to be freight.
Giuliana walked in on Priya and me in the extension earlier — flustered, in a hurry, and holding something silver she very much did not want us to see. She left faster than she came.
The bootlegger checks on those crates the way I check on my daughter. More, actually.
New money, old money — it all spends. The difference is old money hires people so the fingerprints come off.
I gave those acres back with interest and a smile. The smile cost me more than the acres.

characters.signature_item: A house key to his own manor on a gold fob, which he jingles when making a point.
characters.tamper_insert: a gold key fob stamped with the neighboring estate's crest

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: The west wing extension, with Priya Patel, from well before the butler screamed until well after. A gentleman stops the story there — except to say the professor was fussing over crates in the corner the whole time, and a woman with a silver flask burst in on us and left faster than she came. Ask any of them. I'd rather you asked Priya.

questions.prompt: You move freight for a living. What's in those crates out west?
questions.answer: Not Braun's, I'll tell you that. Import stamps, no house inventory tags — freight that doesn't want to be freight. The bootlegger checks on them the way I check on my daughter. More, actually. One of them went out lighter than it came in tonight.

questions.prompt: Is your manor really smaller than this one?
questions.answer: Slightly. Three acres slightly, and for ten years it wasn't. I gave them back with interest and a smile, and the smile cost more than the acres.

characters.name: Priya Patel
characters.voice: Easy country-club charm with a competitor's edge; talks in golf metaphors, laughs off hard questions, and goes very quiet whenever her father comes up.
characters.backstory: You are a rising golf pro with a clean swing and a complicated bloodline — your father was Midnight Syndicate, years ago, before he got out. You have spent your whole career being one tabloid headline away from being his daughter first and an athlete second.
characters.why_invited: Braun sponsors the club championship and collects promising people. You came for the networking and found Cairo Iwobi instead, which was better networking.
characters.dislikes_braun: At a dinner last spring, Braun introduced you to a senator as 'the Syndicate girl who golfs.' He apologized with a case of wine. You kept the wine and the grudge in equal condition.
characters.observable: You were conspicuously absent with Cairo Iwobi in the extension room during the key stretch of the evening, and you answer questions about your father with a practiced, too-smooth deflection.
characters.seen_as: The charming athlete with the dangerous last name — probably innocent, definitely tired of proving it.

life: I've won four tournaments this season. The headline on three of them still mentioned my father. You learn to play through.
I was in the west wing extension for a stretch of the evening. With Cairo. We were not discussing golf, and that's all the detail anyone's getting.

I was in the west wing extension with Cairo Iwobi through the whole stretch everyone keeps asking about — before the butler screamed, and after. We were interrupted once, by Giuliana, holding a little silver flask like it was stolen. Cairo saw it too. Go and check, I'll wait.
weather: Wind like this adds two clubs. Storm reading is half my job — you learn to feel when something's about to break.
The rain hit the extension windows around ten. I remember because it covered the sound of someone moving crates next door. Or I thought it did.

lines: The extension is the most private room in the house, which I can confirm professionally, having tested it.
There's a storage door out west that was bolted at eight and unbolted at ten. I notice lines. Sight lines, fairway lines, bolt lines.
Giuliana burst in on us in the extension, holding a little silver flask shaped like — this will sound insane — a snail. She hid it so fast I almost doubted myself. Almost.
People keep looking at me tonight like the name Patel is evidence. My father sold that life for a driving range. Look at someone who's still buying.
Tour winnings are good; sponsorships are better; a clean reputation is the whole portfolio. Which is why tonight is a problem for me specifically.
The Syndicate offered my father a way back in every year for a decade. He said no every year. Some people at this party never got asked to say no. Think about why.

characters.signature_item: A worn golf glove tucked in her clutch — 'for luck' — with her father's initials inked inside the cuff.
characters.tamper_insert: a worn golf glove, initials inked inside the cuff that don't match the owner's

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: In the west wing extension with Cairo Iwobi, through the whole stretch — before the butler screamed and after. We were not discussing golf. We were interrupted once, by Giuliana, holding a little silver flask like it was stolen. Cairo saw it too. Go and check. I'll wait.

questions.prompt: What's this about a bolted door in the extension?
questions.answer: The storage door out west was bolted at eight and unbolted at ten. I notice lines — sight lines, fairway lines, bolt lines. Somebody used that door while the whole house was watching the stage. It wasn't me. I was busy.

questions.prompt: What's the glove in your clutch for?
questions.answer: Luck. It's my father's old one — his initials inside the cuff, not mine, and yes, I know how that reads tonight. He sold that life for a driving range. Look at someone who's still buying.

characters.name: Solomon Roka
characters.voice: Gravel-and-honey salesman's warmth, always mid-toast, pressing a glass into your hand before you've said hello — and going polite and flat the moment anyone mentions manifests.
characters.backstory: You are the Bootleg King — importer of spirits that skip certain paperwork, distributor for rooms that don't ask. The Midnight Syndicate runs its liquor through you, and Braun's ledger had your routes in it, dated and priced. You knew, because the Syndicate told you, and then told you what tonight required.
characters.why_invited: You supplied the party's bar — crates of it, staged in the west wing — and invited yourself along with the delivery. You spent the front half of the evening in the foyer pouring samples and being magnificent, which is called an alibi.
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun drank your imports for five years and then started writing them down. A customer becoming a witness is the oldest heartbreak in your business, and it only ever ends one way.
characters.observable: You came in through the side, not the front — and you guard the bar crates in the extension room with a geniality that gets less genial the closer anyone stands to them.
characters.seen_as: Everyone's favorite bad influence — the man with the good bottles, the better stories, and no visible supply chain.

life: Forty years moving bottles across borders that disagree with me. Every scar has a vintage.
I was in the foyer half the night pouring my imports for anyone with a glass. Ask around — fifty witnesses, all of them a little happier for it.
My father sold liquor out of a rowboat. I sell it out of freighters. The paperwork is the only part of the business that ever changed, and I never cared for paperwork.
weather: Storm's good for business. Nobody counts their drinks in weather like this, and nobody counts the crates either.
Smell that rain? Petrichor, they call it. Covers almost any other smell in a house. Almost.

lines: My crates are staged in the west extension, and I'll thank the curious to admire them from a distance. Breakage, you understand. I'm very concerned about breakage.
Big house, one bar that matters. Mine. Even Braun's private study got a bottle of the good stuff tonight. A peace offering, you could say.
The reporter's been counting my crates all week like they're going to confess. Paper doesn't drink, Miss Henderson. Paper burns.
The doctor jokes that my brandy is poison. Medical people, no romance in them. It's not poison, madam, it's heritage — with a kick.
Margins in my trade are beautiful because the taxes are theoretical. The overhead is loyalty. Loyalty's gotten expensive lately.
Braun owed me nothing and I owed Braun nothing, and that's exactly how I like my dead men. Poor choice of words. Pour you another?

characters.signature_item: A bottle of his own private label — Roka Reserve, a smoked plum brandy with a distinctive burnt-sweet nose.
characters.tamper_insert: a cork stamped ROKA RESERVE, still damp, smelling of smoked plum
characters.epilogue: Solomon Roka built the Syndicate's routes out of his father's rowboat, and every crate in the west wing was his. Braun had bought his liquor for ten years and written down every delivery, and a bootlegger's ledger in a detective's hands is a noose. So Roka gave up one bottle of his own label — the peace offering that carried the doctor's tincture up to the study — and poured for fifty witnesses while it did its work. He would have preferred a fair fight. He has never been offered one.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: The foyer, pouring my imports for anyone who'd hold a glass out. Fifty witnesses, all of them a little happier for it. I heard glass break and I thought it was a waiter. I kept pouring. The butler's scream is what stopped me.
questions.cover_answer: The foyer, pouring, same as I said — but you're asking the wrong man about the wrong room. {target} took a glass off me at half past nine and walked it toward the study corridor. Never came back for the second. I notice who comes back for the second.

questions.prompt: Did one of your bottles go to the study tonight?
questions.answer: One did. Roka Reserve, my own label, smoked plum — a peace offering to a man who didn't much like me. I handed it to the house to deliver, the way you do. What the house did with it, you'd have to ask the house.
questions.cover_answer: One did, and I didn't carry it. I handed the bottle to {target} to take up, because they offered and I had fifty glasses to fill. If it got opened before it got there, you'll want to ask them, not me.

questions.prompt: How did you get into the liquor business?
questions.answer: My father sold it out of a rowboat. I sell it out of freighters. The paperwork is the only part of the business that ever changed, and I never cared for paperwork.

characters.name: Remington Whitley
characters.voice: Clipped, economical cop cadence — answers in facts, asks in wedges, and lets silences do most of his interrogating.
characters.backstory: You are a twenty-five-year police detective who has chased the Midnight Syndicate your entire career and watched every case die in a drawer. Six months ago, James Braun approached you privately: Braun had a ledger, and he was almost ready to hand it over. PRIVATE — YOUR VENDETTA: One year ago you came home to find your dog dead on your kitchen floor, and a cream-coloured calling card on the counter. No message, just a small snail pressed into the wax. You knew what it meant and you knew who sends cards like that: Giuliana Andolpho. You have never been able to prove it and you have never stopped wanting to. SECONDARY OBJECTIVE: if Giuliana Andolpho is convicted at any trial tonight, you claim your vendetta — worth points in the wider game regardless of how the night ends. This does not replace your job. You still win or lose with the investigators, and she is not one of the three hands, so every vote you spend on her is a vote the town needed elsewhere. That is the price. Decide whether you'll pay it.
characters.why_invited: Braun invited you as insurance. The handoff was set for midnight tonight — the ledger, the names, the whole snail-stamped network. You spent the evening outside, watching the house, because you don't believe in 'almost ready.'
characters.dislikes_braun: Braun sat on that ledger for six months, playing it like a hand of cards — protecting his investments, timing his exit, letting the Syndicate operate while he negotiated his own safety. Men died in those six months. You keep the list.
characters.observable: You spent most of the evening on the lawn and around the cars 'getting air,' and you have a habit of writing in a weatherproof notebook without looking down at it.
characters.seen_as: The cop at the party — nobody's sure if he's off duty, and he has done nothing whatsoever to clarify.

life: Twenty-five years on the job. Nineteen of them chasing one organization. You don't retire from a case like that. It retires you.
I was outside most of the night. Lawn, driveway, the cars. Air. A man my age needs a lot of air.
Braun and I had an appointment at midnight. That's all I'll say. The appointment is now evidence.
weather: Rain kills footprints and softens ground. Whoever moved outside tonight knew that or got lucky. I don't believe in lucky.
I've done stakeouts in worse. In weather like this you watch the windows, because that's where the light tells the truth.

lines: The study windows face the lawn. From the far garden bed you can see Braun's desk lamp. It went out at 9:47. I wrote it down at 9:47.
Four ways to that study. Two halls, one window, one side path. I had eyes on exactly one of them. That's the failure I'll be living with.

The chauffeur left her post at the valet stand mid-evening. Short-answered me when I made small talk, then walked toward the side of the house. People walk away from small talk when the talk is small. Mine wasn't.
The doctor won't meet my eye tonight. Medical people either look right at you or not at all. She's usually the first kind.
A detective's pension is a joke the city tells for thirty years. I'm not in this for money. That makes me rare in this room, and I know it.
The Syndicate's money ends up in liquor, real estate, charity galas, and campaigns. I've said that in four courtrooms. Tonight I'm standing inside all four.

characters.signature_item: A weatherproof stakeout notebook with a rubber band around it, pages warped by tonight's rain.
characters.tamper_insert: a rain-warped page of stakeout notes in a policeman's shorthand
characters.epilogue: Remington Whitley has spent thirty years arriving too late, and tonight he was outside the right window with a notebook and still missed it by one path. He had been waiting for a midnight handoff that never came. What he got instead was the times, in ink, and a room full of dinner guests who did the rest. He will say the case closed itself. It did not.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: Outside. The far garden bed, under the study windows, getting air — a man my age needs a lot of air. I heard glass break at 9:47 and the butler scream at 9:50, and I wrote both down. I write everything down. Some of it I understand later.

questions.prompt: What's in the notebook you keep writing in without looking?
questions.answer: Times. The singer took the stage at 9:40 and the hall filled. A figure on the side path at 9:41, small build, carrying something. Glass breaking in the study at 9:47, and the lamp out right after. The butler's scream at 9:50. The same figure coming back at 9:54, still carrying. Four ways into that study and I had eyes on one. That's the failure I'll be living with.

questions.prompt: Off duty tonight, or on?
questions.answer: A detective's never off. I'm not here for money, which makes me rare in this room, and I know it.

characters.name: Carla Lucciano
characters.voice: Flat, watchful economy of words — service-industry politeness worn thin, with sudden dry humor and a habit of answering questions with slightly wrong questions.
characters.backstory: You have been Braun's chauffeur for four years — and the Midnight Syndicate's for eleven. You were placed in this house the way the Syndicate places people: patiently. You know every route, every door, every schedule, and tonight you used all three.
characters.why_invited: Staff. You ran the valet stand, directed the cars, and controlled the one stretch of ground nobody watches: the side path that wraps from the driveway to the study wall.
characters.dislikes_braun: Four years of 'the car, Carla' and not one full sentence besides. Being furniture was the job — the Syndicate's whole point — but somewhere in year two, being invisible stopped being tactical and started being personal to you.
characters.observable: You were away from the valet stand between roughly 9:35 and 9:50; you keep your driving gloves on indoors and went short and impatient with anyone who made small talk near the cars.
characters.seen_as: Part of the house — competent, unreadable, and the person who knows exactly who arrived when, and how.

life: Four years driving this family. You learn a house from the outside in. The outside is more honest.
I was at the valet stand most of the night. Most of it. Cars don't park themselves and guests don't stop arriving. Ask anyone. Ask them what time, though, and watch them guess.
Before this I drove for other people. The kind you don't put on a resume. Everyone's driven for somebody.
weather: Rain means twenty umbrella runs and ruined gravel. The side path holds footprints in weather like this. So I raked it. That's called doing my job.
Storm rolled in right on schedule. Some things tonight ran very on schedule.

lines: The side path wraps from the driveway to the study side of the house. Staff use it. Deliveries use it. It's not a secret, it's just never watched.
I hold keys to every door on this property. That's not suspicious, that's the job description. Read the job description before you look at me like that.
The trainee detective checked the valet stand twice tonight like I wouldn't notice. I notice everything on my driveway. It's my driveway.
I escorted a late arrival around the side earlier — party business, staff business. Guests who reek of brandy don't go through the front. House rule. Braun's own rule, if you want the irony.
Driver's wages are what they are. The benefits package is knowing everyone's schedule. Some employers value that more than others.
Eleven years I've been paid by people who plan in decades. Braun paid me for four of them. Guess whose money arrived first.

characters.signature_item: A master key ring for the house and cars, worn on her belt — including a study passkey she signed out tonight and quietly returned.
characters.tamper_insert: a driver's leather glove, sized small, smelling faintly of smoked plum brandy
characters.epilogue: Carla Lucciano drove for the Syndicate for eleven years before she drove for the Brauns, and the family never asked where she had learned to keep her eyes forward. She holds every key on the property, knows which path the rain wipes clean, and was the only one of the three willing to walk through the study door. She did it because the Syndicate told her to, and because in her experience people who refuse the Syndicate stop being people. She raked the path afterward. It is her job.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
questions.answer: Walking a late guest round the side of the house. He reeked of brandy, and guests who reek don't go through the front — Braun's own rule. Then I raked the path, because the rain had it like soup. I heard the butler scream from out there. I was back at the stand before anyone missed me, apart from the trainee, who counts.
questions.cover_answer: Walking a late guest round the side, and I wasn't the only one on that path. {target} came down it toward the study door while I was raking, quick, head down, and told me to mind my own business when I asked. So I did. Now I'm telling you.

questions.prompt: You signed the study passkey out at 9:33. Why?
questions.answer: Because Braun asked for a bottle to be put in his study before ten, and the house was short-handed with everyone in the hall. I let myself in, left it on the desk, locked up, and signed it back at 9:56. It's in the log in my own initials. Thieves don't keep logs.
questions.cover_answer: Because {target} asked me to. Came to the stand at half past nine, said Braun wanted something taken up and could I open the study door — I hold every key on this property, it's the job. I opened it. I did not go in. Whoever did, you should ask them what they were carrying.

questions.prompt: Why do you keep your driving gloves on indoors?
questions.answer: Habit. Four years driving this family, eleven driving for people you don't put on a résumé. The gloves stay on.

characters.name: Harry Braun
characters.voice: Bitter aristocratic drawl running on fumes and cigarettes — the accent of money delivered by a man who no longer has any, every sentence a toast to his own ruin.
characters.backstory: You are James Braun's older, estranged brother — written out of the family estate nine years ago after 'the incident with the trust,' which you maintain was a misunderstanding involving only slightly forged signatures. You have been circling the family fortune ever since like weather.
characters.why_invited: Nobody is sure you were. The invitation you showed at the door looks real from a distance, which is also a fair description of you.
characters.dislikes_braun: James got the house, the money, the name — and then got to play the wounded party when you took what any starving man takes. Nine years of Christmas cards with no checks in them. The engagement was the last insult: a new heir incoming, and your claim dissolving in champagne.
characters.observable: You chain-smoked outside near the entry for long stretches of the evening, and you pat your breast pocket compulsively — there's a folded document in there you keep touching and not showing anyone.
characters.seen_as: The disgraced brother — charming at fifty paces, radioactive at five, and very obviously here for the will.

life: I'm the elder Braun, in case the resemblance escaped you. Older by three years and poorer by nine.
I stepped out to smoke by the entry more times than I can count tonight. The house makes my chest tight. Always has. Even before it wasn't mine.
The incident with the trust was a misunderstanding between me, a pen, and my brother's lawyers. Two of the three refused to be reasonable.
weather: A storm at a Braun party. Grandfather would have called it the family showing up.
I smoked through the worst of the rain under the portico. Alone. Which is both my alibi and my biography.

lines: I grew up in this house. That corridor to the study? I used to hide in it. I know which floorboard doesn't creak. I resent that you're now wondering about that.
Everything in the family room cabinets used to be half mine. I've counted. Tonight I recounted.

The chauffeur walked a late guest around the side of the house earlier — some fellow absolutely marinated in brandy fumes. The rest of us waited at the front like livestock while she did it. I remember thinking: since when does this house have a brandy entrance?
The fiancee looks at me like I'm the threat to the estate. Madam, I'm the tradition.
I have the family crest, the family stories, and the family nose. The family money went to my brother, along with the family's sense of humor.
There's a document in my pocket that certain lawyers will find very interesting tomorrow. Tonight it's just paper. Tomorrow, we'll see.

characters.signature_item: A silver cigarette case with the Braun family crest, which he was pointedly not allowed to keep and kept anyway.
characters.tamper_insert: a crested silver cigarette case, the Braun family arms worn nearly smooth
characters.epilogue: Harry Braun grew up in this house and was written out of it twice: once by his father and once by his brother. He came tonight with a document in his breast pocket and a cigarette in his hand, and he has never pretended to grieve. The estate was always going to go to whichever Braun was left standing. He would have preferred it to be him without help. He will take it with.

questions.prompt: Where were you when Braun was murdered?
